{{Short description|Concept in economics and game theory}}
{{see also|Globle (game)}}
In [[economics]] and [[game theory]], '''global games''' are games of incomplete information where players receive possibly-correlated signals of the underlying state of the world. Global games were originally defined by Carlsson and [[Eric van Damme|van Damme]] (1993).<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Hans |last1=Carlsson |first2=Eric |last2=van Damme |year=1993 |title=Global Games and Equilibrium Selection |journal=Econometrica |volume=61 |issue=5 |pages=989–1018 |doi=10.2307/2951491 |jstor=2951491 |url=http://www.dklevine.com/archive/refs4122247000000001088.pdf }}</ref>

The most important practical application of global games has been the study of [[Financial crisis|crises in financial markets]] such as [[banking crisis|bank runs]], [[currency crisis|currency crises]], and [[bubble (economics)|bubbles]]. However, they have other relevant applications such as investments with payoff complementarities, [[beauty contests]], [[political riots]] and [[revolutions]], and any other economic situation which displays [[strategic complementarity]].

== Global games in models of currency crises ==
[[Stephen Morris (game theorist)|Stephen Morris]] and [[Hyun Song Shin]] (1998) considered a stylized currency crises model, in which traders observe the relevant fundamentals with small noise, and show that this leads to the selection of a unique equilibrium.<ref>{{cite journal |first1=Stephen |last1=Morris |first2=Hyun Song |last2=Shin |year=1998 |title=Unique Equilibrium in a Model of Self-Fulfilling Currency Attacks |journal=American Economic Review |volume=88 |issue=3 |pages=587–97 |jstor=116850 }}</ref> This result overturns the result in models of [[complete information]], which feature multiple equilibria.

One concern with the robustness of this result is that the introduction of a theory of prices in global coordination games may reintroduce multiplicity of equilibria.<ref name="Atkeson, 2001">{{cite book |first=Andrew G. |last=Atkeson |year=2001 |chapter=Rethinking Multiple Equilibria in Macroeconomic Modeling: Comment |title=[[National Bureau of Economic Research|NBER]] Macroeconomics Annual 2000 |editor-first=Ben S. |editor-last=Bernanke |editor-link=Ben S. Bernanke |editor2-first=Kenneth |editor2-last=Rogoff |editor2-link=Kenneth Rogoff |pages=162–71 |location=Cambridge, MA |publisher=[[MIT Press]] }}</ref> This concern was addressed in [[George-Marios Angeletos|Angeletos]] and [[Iván Werning|Werning]] (2006) as well as [[Christian Hellwig|Hellwig]] and coauthors (2006).<ref>{{cite journal |first1=George-Marios |last1=Angeletos |first2=Ivan |last2=Werning |year=2006 |title=Crises and Prices: Information Aggregation, Multiplicity, and Volatility |journal=American Economic Review |volume=96 |issue=5 |pages=1720–36 |doi=10.1257/aer.96.5.1720 |hdl=1721.1/63311 |hdl-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |first1=Christian |last1=Hellwig |first2=Arijit |last2=Mukherji |first3=Aleh |last3=Tsyvinski |year=2006 |title=Self-Fulfilling Currency Crises: The Role of Interest Rates |journal=American Economic Review |volume=96 |issue=5 |pages=1769–1787 |doi=10.1257/aer.96.5.1769 |url=http://www.nber.org/papers/w11191.pdf }}</ref> They show that equilibrium multiplicity may be restored by the existence of prices acting as an endogenous public signal, provided that [[privacy|private information]] is sufficiently precise.
